source.title: The Effects of Regularization and Data Augmentation are Class Dependent
source.authors: Randall Balestriero; L. Bottou; Yann LeCun

page_placements.theme: Augmentation depends on views, transformations and evaluation

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text includes the paper and supplementary material.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports experiments on how regularization changes class-specific test performance, using a different measure and question from the listed claim versions. Its results do not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on class-dependent test accuracy under data augmentation and weight decay. It does not report results on memorizing random labels, widening past interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected networks, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout, sharpness measures, or removing memorized examples. Figures provide most class-level outcomes; cited prior work is not extracted as a result.
record.test_reason: The study measures class-dependent effects of random-crop augmentation and weight decay, including transfer learning. None of V1–V8 names these comparisons. In particular, weight-decay experiments without a dropout comparison do not test V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: augmentation and weight decay can improve average performance while harming particular classes. Transfer of class-dependent effects is demonstrated specifically for random-crop augmentation during ImageNet pre-training with a frozen backbone on INaturalist.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments vary data augmentation and weight decay and measure class-specific test performance; they do not reproduce the methods or measurements in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Per-class test performance varies with the random crop lower bound and with the weight decay coefficient; the transfer experiment also varies the pre-training crop lower bound.

fits_no_version.finding: Stronger random cropping increases average ImageNet accuracy while academic-gown accuracy falls from 62% to 40%; the authors report evidence of harm for 4.4% of classes at their 95% testing threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-crop augmentation can improve average accuracy while reducing accuracy on particular classes.

fits_no_version.finding: ImageNet classes respond differently to weight decay, with some improving and others worsening.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay can change class-specific test accuracy in different directions.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing pre-training cropping changes downstream class accuracy with a frozen backbone; the abstract reports a 70% to 30% decrease for INaturalist class #8889.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Augmentation during pre-training can produce class-dependent accuracy changes on downstream tasks.

record.code_released: Codes, full result tables, and pre-trained model weights will be released soon
record.problems: Most class-level outcomes are presented only in figures, so precise per-class values cannot be extracted from the supplied text. The significance result is reported as a percentage of classes rather than class-by-class estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional outcomes were left out. Other figure trends are described qualitatively but do not provide a separately stated numerical value or distinct outcome suitable for an additional row.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, dataset-size and dropout-strength dependencies, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a correlate of generalization gaps and its ranking against other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T2 classification conflicts with its own explanation and should be discusses/T6. Row states are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; the study does establish the separate effects described under fits_no_version. No verdict labels apply.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance on natural labels.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Dropout's effect on held-out error and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with the train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with horizontal flip and random crop using varying crop lower bounds.
rows.note: The text states that stronger random crop augmentation increases average test accuracy; exact values are only shown in the figure.
rows.check: The reported increase in average accuracy concerns augmentation strength, not any listed version. Horizontal flipping is used throughout.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3, Figure 4 caption and accompanying paragraph, p. 6.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with random crop augmentation at varying lower bounds.
rows.note: The paper says accuracy falls steadily as τ decreases.
rows.check: The 62% to 40% decrease is correctly extracted, but it is not a reversal of any listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Compared training with no data augmentation against random crop augmentation with α ∈ [100, 8].
rows.measure: Share of classes for which evidence supports higher mean accuracy without augmentation
rows.baseline: No augmentation versus random crop augmentation
rows.note: The paper reports that this share is 2.1% at 99% confidence.
rows.check: The 4.4% result concerns class-specific harm from random cropping. Describe the comparator as no random cropping: Figure 4 retains horizontal flipping. The 95% figure is the authors' per-class testing threshold, not a confidence interval on the proportion of affected classes.

source_check.correct: The comparator omits random cropping, while retaining horizontal flipping; the treatment adds random cropping with an 8% lower bound. The reported share is 4.4% at the authors' 95% per-class testing threshold, and 2.1% at 99%.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3, Figure 4 caption and statistical-test paragraphs, p. 6.
source_check.problem: The baseline and training-operation description incorrectly say no data augmentation; horizontal flipping remains enabled.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with varying weight decay coefficients.
rows.note: The text says different classes have different sensitivities, with some improving and others decreasing as weight decay varies.
rows.check: Varying weight decay alone does not test V6's dropout comparisons or joint removal of dropout and weight decay. The text reports mixed directions across classes.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained on ImageNet; transferred to INaturalist with frozen backbone
rows.operation_detail: Pre-trained with varying random crop lower bounds, then trained a linear classifier on the target dataset.
rows.note: The authors report class-dependent performance varying with the pre-training crop lower bound; exact class values are only shown in the figure.
rows.check: The transfer result fits no listed version. The figure-only value description overlooks the abstract's numerical example: INaturalist class #8889 accuracy falls from 70% to 30% when random cropping is introduced during ImageNet pre-training.

relation.reason: The paper discusses regularization and generalization, but its comparisons do not test V1–V8; in particular, it has no dropout comparison for V6.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure class-dependent effects of random cropping and weight decay, without testing or using any listed version's specific finding.
